section_summary: This section consists of a two-page intelligence report (Report No. 10,257) dated December 12, 1940, from Lieutenant Colonel Harry I. T. Creswell, the U.S. Military Attaché in Tokyo. The report analyzes Japanese press and public reactions to the announcement of a $100,000,000 U.S. loan to Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government alongside Japan's treaty with the Wang Ching-wei regime, concluding that strong nationalist sentiment will ensure public support for leadership despite fears of war with the United States. It also assesses intelligence on difficult Russo-Japanese negotiations in Moscow, focusing on Soviet demands regarding Northern Sakhalin oil concessions, fisheries, and continued Soviet aid to China.

subfiles.about: Intelligence report on Japanese press and public reaction to the U.S. loan to China and the status of Soviet-Japanese negotiations in Moscow.
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, Lieutenant Colonel, Acting General Staff, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Harry I. T. Creswell analyzes Japanese reactions to the simultaneous announcement of a $100,000,000 American loan to Chiang Kai-shek and Japan's treaty with Wang Ching-wei, noting press indignation at U.S. alignment with Great Britain against the Axis. While moderate Japanese elements deplore deteriorating relations and fear conflict, deep-seated nationalism and conviction in the necessity of victory in China ensure that the public will follow national leadership in any crisis. The report also details rumors that Russo-Japanese accord talks in Moscow are stalled by Soviet demands for the return of Northern Sakhalin oil leases, revised fishing arrangements, and a refusal to cease aid to China.
